---
title: "Selectors and roles"
---

Recipe steps operate on columns of data, which are specified using Polars selectors.
While Polars selectors can specify pieces like all numeric columns (`cs.numeric()`),
they can't target modelling pieces like all "feature" columns.
mlfeatures enables this by adding Roles, modelling specific labels for columns and selectors to target them.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Key points"}
- A step accepts a column name, a list of names, a polars or narwhals
  selector, or a mlfeatures selector from `Selectors`, imported as `s`.
- mlfeatures selectors choose by name, type, role, or the step that produced a
  column, and compose with `&`, `|`, `~`, and `-`.
- `Recipe(..., target="col")` gives a column the `target` role, which keeps it
  out of feature selectors like `s.numeric_features()`.
- `Recipe.summary()` lists every column with its dtype, roles, and the step
  that produced it.
- Every non-target column is a feature by default; `features=` names them
  explicitly, and `case_weights` columns are never features.
- `set_roles()` attaches custom roles, and `s.has_role()` selects by them.
:::

## Setup

The examples use two datasets from `mlfeatures.data`: the credit data, whose
target is a string, and a small Ames housing subset, whose target is
numeric.

```{python}
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

from mlfeatures import Recipe, StepDummy, StepImputeMedian, StepNormalize
from mlfeatures import Selectors as s
from mlfeatures.data import ames_mini, credit
```

## Selector basics

Pass a polars selector, or a mlfeatures selector from `s`, wherever a step takes
columns. mlfeatures selectors cover the same name and type checks
(`s.numeric()`, `s.starts_with()`, `s.col()`) and compose with set
operators, so "every numeric column except `Price`" is one expression.

```{python}
recipe = (
    Recipe(data=credit, target="Status")
    .add(StepImputeMedian(cs.numeric()))  # polars selector
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric() - s.col("Price")))  # mlfeatures selector
)
fitted = recipe.fit(credit)
fitted
```

A selector is resolved when the recipe is fitted, against the columns that
exist at that point in the pipeline. That is why the fitted recipe lists
concrete names, why the same selector works on any backend, and why a later
step can pick up columns an earlier step created. The full set is on the
`Selectors` reference page.

## Roles: features and targets

Use `Recipe(..., target="col")` to give a column the `target` role, which
excludes it from the mlfeatures feature selectors such as `s.numeric_features()`.
A polars selector like `cs.numeric()` knows nothing about roles, so it
includes the target:

```{python}
recipe = (
    Recipe(data=ames_mini, target="Sale_Price")
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features()))  # excludes target
    .add(StepNormalize(cs.numeric()))  # includes target
)
fitted = recipe.fit(ames_mini)
fitted
```

`s.numeric_features()` is simply `s.numeric()` restricted to the `feature`
role. The `_features` variants exist for each type (`s.nominal_features()`,
`s.date_features()`, and so on), and `s.features()` and `s.targets()` select
by role alone.

## Roles: specifying features

Every column that is not the target is a feature by default, so a feature
selector sees all of them. Pass `features=` to name the features yourself:
the other columns then carry no role, so selectors ignore them, and
`transform()` passes them through unchanged.

```{python}
recipe = Recipe(
    data=ames_mini,
    target="Sale_Price",
    features=["Gr_Liv_Area", "Year_Built", "Neighborhood"],
).add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features()))
fitted = recipe.fit(ames_mini)
fitted
```

The default is applied when the recipe is fitted, which is why an untrained
recipe with only a target reports just that target. One standard role is
never a feature: a column declared `case_weights=` holds per-sample weights
and is left out of every feature selector.

## Displaying role information

`Recipe.summary()` lists one row per column with its dtype, its roles, and
the step that produced it, so after a dummy step the indicator columns show
up as features whose source is `dummy`:

```{python}
recipe = (
    Recipe(data=ames_mini, target="Sale_Price")
    .add(StepDummy(s.nominal_features()))
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features()))
)
fitted = recipe.fit(ames_mini)
fitted.summary()
```

## Custom roles

`set_roles(name=[...])` attaches any custom role, a column can carry several
roles at once, and `s.has_role()` selects by one. Tagging `Latitude` and
`Longitude` as `geo` keeps them out of normalization while they stay
features:

```{python}
recipe = (
    Recipe(data=ames_mini, target="Sale_Price")
    .set_roles(geo=["Latitude", "Longitude"])
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features() - s.has_role("geo")))
)
fitted = recipe.fit(ames_mini)
fitted.summary().filter(pl.col("roles").str.contains("geo"))
```

## Changing roles part way through

`set_roles()` labels the columns that arrive with the data, and it does so
whatever its position in the recipe. To change a role at a point in the
pipeline, use `add_role()`, `update_role()` or `remove_role()`. Each takes
effect where it is written: the steps after it see the new role, the steps
before it do not, and it can reach columns that earlier steps created.
Here the dummy indicators get an `indicator` role, which the normalization
that follows leaves out by selecting features without it:

```{python}
recipe = (
    Recipe(data=ames_mini, target="Sale_Price")
    .add(StepDummy(s.nominal_features()))
    .add_role(s.has_source("dummy"), role="indicator")
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features() - s.has_role("indicator")))
)
fitted = recipe.fit(ames_mini)
fitted.summary().filter(pl.col("roles").str.contains("indicator"))
```

`update_role(columns, new_role=..., old_role=...)` swaps one role for another,
or replaces all of a column's roles when `old_role` is left out, and
`remove_role(columns, role=...)` takes a role away. Like a step's `columns`,
the first argument can be a name, a list of names, or a selector.
